claims.text: Brittle behavior in compositionally complex HEAs emerges through nanoscale grain-boundary segregation rather than coarse intermetallic precipitation.
Prolonged exposure to service-relevant temperatures causes specific alloying elements to diffuse to and segregate at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation produces local chemical fluctuations and incipient short-range ordering.
The local chemical fluctuations and short-range ordering reduce grain-boundary cohesion and promote brittle fracture.
The initial HEA is single-phase, chemically uniform, and free of detectable secondary phases or coarse precipitates after rapid solidification and solution treatment.
Aging at 700–900°C is sufficient to promote elemental diffusion and grain-boundary segregation in the HEA.
A conventional alloy exposed under identical conditions will embrittle by forming coarse, brittle grain-boundary precipitates.
Differential diffusion of multiple alloying species during high-temperature exposure causes selected elements to accumulate at HEA grain boundaries without forming obvious precipitates.
Minor grain-boundary segregation lowers interfacial cohesive strength.
Lower grain-boundary cohesive strength causes brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
Coarse brittle intermetallic particles are the distinguishing, readily detectable embrittlement mechanism in the conventional-alloy control.
Relative to the unaged baseline, the aged HEA will exhibit lower Charpy impact energy.
Aging will change the HEA fracture surface from ductile dimples to brittle cleavage features.
Nanoscale characterization will detect subtle grain-boundary segregation in the aged HEA that correlates with its loss of toughness.
The unaged as-cast or solution-treated HEA has favorable strength–ductility performance and no grain-boundary embrittlement.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate during aging at 700–900°C and under loading, particularly low-temperature impact loading, that promotes brittle fracture.
The mechanism may not operate outside the stated thermal or mechanical window or when service conditions limit grain-boundary diffusion.
Matched HEA and conventional-alloy specimens should be aged under identical conditions and compared using atom probe tomography, TEM, Charpy testing, tensile testing, and fractography.
Absence of meaningful segregation or short-range ordering, together with unchanged toughness and fracture behavior after aging, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Formation of similar coarse precipitates in both the HEA and conventional-alloy control would refute the claimed mechanistic distinction.

contradictions.description: The mechanism centers on reduced grain-boundary cohesion, which most directly predicts intergranular separation, but the predicted fracture signature is cleavage, a transgranular mode. The hypothesis does not explain this mismatch or specify whether intergranular fracture is also expected.
